senses: A form of music originating in Argentina, Uruguay, and Southern Brazil.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish milonga, in turn from Brazilian Portuguese milonga (“chant”). Theories connect the word to the nineteenth century slave trade between South America and Africa. The ultimate source is unknown, but may relate to Kimbundu mulonga (“word”), or Kongo nlonga or Punu mulonga (“line, row”) in reference to dancers.
examples: In “Gath & Chaves,” a section named after a department store, women pose as mannequins but come to life to dance a tango, a waltz, a milonga and, finally, a mystifying number called “Hound Dog.”

senses: A container hidden in a specific location during geocaching.
ety: From geo- + cache. Suggested by participants in the mailing list gpsstash@egroups.com in May 2000, replacing the earlier gpsstash (see quotations below).
examples: The treasures in this case are geocaches, those little plastic boxes of goodies that are hidden all over the earth.
With school out for the summer, Jason and Sarah sat down and mapped a strategy to find the geocaches at each of the state's seventy-two parks and recreation areas.

senses: A certificate of accomplishment given to pilgrims on completing an official route on the pilgramage to Camino de Santiago.
ety: From Spanish Compostela, from Galician Compostela, from Latin compositella (“the little well-organized one”), from composita (“put together, arranged”) + -ella (“-elle: forming diminutives”), from compōnere (“to put together”), from con- (“with, together”) + pōnere (“to put, to place”), q.v.

senses: A kind of soft white cheese.
The process of aggregating or coalescing into a mass.
A solid, hard mass formed by a process of aggregation or coalescence.
The action of making something concrete or the result of such an action.
ety: Borrowed from French concrétion, or Latin concretio.

senses: A person who uses dynamite, especially one who uses it unlawfully.
Involving conflict or difficulties
One who is involved in the creation or dissemination of pornography.
That originates in the tissues of the teeth
Having the quality of dissolving in lipids; typically composed of mostly nonpolar bonds.
a subdivision of a barangay, typically rural.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish sitio. Doublet of site and situs.

senses: A form of historical Spanish or Italian dance characterised by a serious nature, triple meter, and use of a ground bass.
Any piece of classical music with similar characteristics.
ety: Borrowed from Italian passacaglia, from Spanish pasacalle, from pasar (“to pass”) + calle (“street”).

senses: A rose cultivar, having large sprays of small flowers, made by crossing polyantha and hybrid tea rose varieties.
A refrigerator adapted for storing and serving beer from a keg.
examples: He will be on your side when you want to spend an entire Saturday making the house smell like a brewery or drop several hundred dollars to build a kegerator.

senses: Synonym of monarchical.
ety: Probably partly from monarchy + -al (compare Middle French monarchial) and partly monarch + -ial.

senses: A dagger used in Tibetan ritual.
A device consisting of two volume controls which control separate records, allowing the DJ to change the source of the sound between the records.
The study of mammals.
Prone to nag, irritable.
Decorated with a banner or banners.
A type of cat native to Southern Africa, West Asia, and parts of Central and South Asia, Caracal caracal.
ety: From French caracal, from Ottoman Turkish قره قولاق (kara kulak, literally “black ear”), a calque of Classical Persian سیاهگوش (siyāh-gōš). Compare modern Turkish karakulak.

senses: A state of nature; conformity to nature.
The doctrine that denies a supernatural agency in the miracles and revelations recorded in religious texts and in spiritual influences.
Any system of philosophy which refers the phenomena of nature as a blind force or forces acting necessarily or according to fixed laws, excluding origination or direction by a will.
A doctrine which denies a strong separation between scientific and philosophic methodologies and/or topics
A cut of beef from the lower part of the back, where the last ribs are (called rump in UK English).
A cut of beef from the middle of the back (corresponding to short loin and partly rib in US English).
ety: From Middle English surloine, from Old French surlonge, from sur la longe (literally “above the loin”).

senses: Any of numerous small, mouselike, chiefly nocturnal, mammals of the family Soricidae.
Certain other small mammals that resemble true shrews.
ety: From Middle English schrewe, from Old English sċrēawa (“shrew”), from Proto-Germanic *skrawwaz (“thin; meagre; frail”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut; shorten; skimp”). Cognates include Old High German scrawaz (“dwarf”), Norwegian skrugg (“dwarf”).

senses: A vehicle with a telescopically extensible boom, which can be fitted with various lifting or manipulative devices such as pallet forks or grab.
ety: From tele- + handler, from telescopic handler.

senses: One who themes something.
An entry in a crossword that forms part of the theme.
examples: The first of the themers is SPARRING PARTNER (“Opponent who helps train a boxer”) — which, as the revealer indicates, includes the word PAR twice.

I threw in a bonus with ASTHMA – Longest familiar word in the English language that begins and ends with a vowel with no vowels in between (though you may not want to use that clue since there is no symmetrical themer).
One themer that ended up on the cutting room floor here is HEADSPACE, a word I find myself using pretty often (e.g. "I'm not in the right HEADSPACE for that right now").

senses: Anything that restricts
Someone who is on vacation
The inner curvature of a ski or snowboard that allows smoother turning.
A type of haircut where the hair is partially shaved on one side.
A visual novel with erotic content.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese エロゲ (eroge) (less commonly エロゲー (erogē)), a shortening of エロチックゲーム (erochikku gēmu), from English erotic game.

senses: A fire extinguisher.
A small hollow conical instrument for putting out a candle.
Exhibiting side, or unjustified self-importance; arrogant.
Insignificant; small-time.
A Tex-Mex dish of strips of spicy marinated meat and/or vegetables in a soft flour tortilla, often served with salad or a savoury filling.
ety: From American Spanish fajita, diminutive of faja (“strip, band”).

senses: The office or dignity of a shogun.
ety: From shogun + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office).

senses: The property of being a loyalist.
ety: From loyal + -ism. Piecewise doublet of legalism.

senses: The vulva or vagina of a trans man, or the neovagina of a detransitioned man.
An obnoxious or contemptible person; a crybaby.
ety: Alteration of earlier gibone (also spelled jiboney, jaboney, etc.), possibly from dialectal Italian giambone (“ham”, also “self-important fool”). As a wrestling term, it was popularized by Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson, who claimed to have borrowed it from the Iron Sheik. Prior to its popularization by Johnson, the term had also been used by Scott Hall, Hulk Hogan, Steve Austin, and others.

senses: A person or machine responsible for managing a mineshaft cage.
A basketball player, from the time when games were played in a wire mesh enclosure.
An area used for saltmaking, especially in the East Anglian fenlands.
A modern saltworks.
ety: From Old English sealtærn, from sealt (“salt”) + ærn (“place, building”).

senses: hagiographic
